paper_title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Small language models are attractive for narrow parsing tasks: they fine-tune in minutes, run on laptop or tablet, and cost almost nothing per call. Their weakness is reliability (Ji et al., 2023), and in structured prediction an error comes in two kinds. An output that does not parse, or that the model marks as refusal, is detectable: the caller rejects it and asks again. An output that parses into plausible tree that is not what the customer said is silent: the order goes through, wrong. This paper treats the silent error rate as the quantity deployment should minimise, and reports exact match beside it for comparison with prior work (Section 5). 1 The work began with deployed café ordering parser whose compact output format was chosen for speed; its small hand-written test set could not tell formats apart, so we moved to public benchmark with human-written test set. Our question is whether the target format is itself lever on silent errors. The same tree can be written as an s-expression, as JSON, as key=value pairs, as terse symbolic language or as plain words, and the choice changes how many tokens the model emits and how much of its pretraining it can reuse. The intuitive hypothesis, that fewer output tokens leave less room for error, turns out to be wrong in the form we first stated it. Shortening helps only when the surface stays in natural words. Contributions. (1) ladder of six lossless encodings of the PIZZA target tree (Arkoudas et al., 2022), with two matched-length pairs that separate length from surface form (Section 4). (2) Evidence across two model families, five pool sizes and five seeds that length alone is not the mechanism: the word encoding beats its symbolic twin of equal length in 10 of 10 modelsize cells, separating in 9 after Holm correction, and on LFM2 it wins while costing more tokens (Section 6.2). (3) The silent error rate as the deployment objective, inside four-way split of every test set. The word encoding has the lowest on both models, and an error analysis shows where the difference comes from (Section 6.3). (4) guardrail trained into every run, refusing off-menu input and applying spoken self-corrections, with its benefit and its cost measured on held-out data (Section 6.4). Code, analysis scripts and the trained models are released at https://github.com/UmarGit/coffee-llm.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Target representation. That the meaning representation affects parser is long established: Dong and Lapata (2016) decode logical forms as trees rather than sequences, and seq2seq parsers for taskoriented dialogue generate the target directly (Rongali et al., 2020). Closest to us, Shin et al. (2021) show that frozen language model prompted to produce canonical natural-language form, mapped to the representation by grammar, beats prompting for the representation itself. We find the same phenomenon under fine-tuning, where the model is free to learn any notation, and we separate naturalness from length with matched pairs and two vocabularies. Format restrictions and constrained decoding. Tam et al. (2024) find that forcing an LLM into JSON costs reasoning accuracy. Constrained decoding makes invalid output impossible (Scholak et al., 2021; Geng et al., 2023; Willard and Louf, 2023); it can remove our unparseable outputs, but it cannot make well-formed tree correct, so the silent rate is the part of the problem it does not reach. Abstention and self-correction. Knowing when not to answer has been studied for reading comprehension (Rajpurkar et al., 2018) and under domain shift (Kamath et al., 2020). Spoken self-repair is classic topic in disfluency research (Shriberg, 1994), and Disfl-QA shows that disfluent input breaks QA models (Gupta et al., 2021). Taskoriented parsing datasets such as TOP, TOPv2 and MTOP (Gupta et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021), and PIZZA itself, contain neither offdomain refusals nor self-corrections; we add both as synthetic training data and evaluate them on held-out vocabulary and cue phrases. Tokenization and evaluation. Subword segmentation (Sennrich et al., 2016) sets what string costs, and vocabulary fit moves accuracy (Rust et al., 2021). We follow recommendations to report seed variance and significance (Dror et al., 2018; Bouthillier et al., 2021), using bootstrap (Efron and Tibshirani, 1993) with Holms correction (Holm, 1979). (2026) Deployment. Ahmed et al. run the WORDS model studied here inside web browser and check that the deployed model reproduces its server evaluation; that work is about the web system and reports no comparison between formats.

sections.title: 3 Task and Data
sections.content: PIZZA (Arkoudas et al., 2022) maps spoken pizza and drink orders to trees with an unordered exactmatch criterion. Its training pool of 2,456,446 utterances is generated from grammar; the 348utterance development set and the 1,357-utterance test set are written by people, which makes the test set the strongest evidence in this paper. The pool contains 3 rows identical to development or test utterance. We drop them from training, and verify on every training subset we draw, at every size and seed, that no evaluation utterance remains, exactly or after normalisation. The splits are used as published. Refusals. PIZZA has no notion of not an order: model trained on it turns hehe hehe into pizza. We add generated negatives making up 30% of every training set: chatter, off-menu requests, gibberish, long text, and real orders with an offmenu clause or an unknown word inserted. The rule is strict: anything that is not purely an order is refused whole. Each format has one short refusal string that cannot parse as an order in that format (? for the three word-like formats, (REJECT ), (R) and {"reject":true} for the others), so all formats train on identical inputs. Vocabulary is split: the 614 evaluation negatives use words never seen in training. Self-corrections. PIZZA has no self-corrections either, so pizza with cheese, wait no cheese, only tomato sauce comes out with both cheese and no cheese. We take real training orders, edit their tree, and append the spoken correction in nine kinds (swap, retract, only, size, number, drink, cancel, restart, and decoys in which cue word changes nothing), adding 10% of the real orders. quarter of the cue phrases are held out: the 600 evaluation corrections are test orders with held-out cues. fixed set of 40 hand-written probes includes the cheese example above, which user reported against an earlier model. Dev and test remain pure PIZZA, so and keep their meaning.

sections.content: Comparing unrelated formats confounds length with form, so we built six encodings of the identical tree that decode back to it on every dev and test utterance and on 50,000-row training sample  (Table 1)  . For each format the upper bar has one box per token and the lower bar draws the same tokens as wide as their characters (both bars to common scale across formats). EXRSHORT renames EXRs constructors to single letters. TAGGED is flat key=value pairs. DSL is terse grammar with sigils (+ for an extra quantity, ! for negation), and WORDS has the same structure as DSL with the markers written as ordinary words; it is DSLs matched-length control. EXR, EXR-SHORT, TAGGED and DSL form length ladder. Characters are not tokens. Over the 1,357 gold test trees, WORDS is the longer of the matched pair in characters (43.1 vs. 34.9) but costs fewer Qwen tokens (10.3 vs. 10.8) and about the same number of LFM2 tokens (11.9 vs. 11.7; Appendix Table 7). LFM2s vocabulary is smaller and inflates the punctuation-heavy formats most (JSON 45.664.7 tokens, WORDS 10.311.9). 3 Models and training. Qwen3.5-0.8B (Yang et al., 2025) and LFM2.5-350M (Amini et al., 2025), largely convolutional model with vocabulary about four times smaller. LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) with rank 16 and α=16 on all linear projections, batch 16, cosine schedule, loss on the completion only. Rank is held fixed across formats because the comparison is between formats, not adapters; Hu et al. (2022) found far lower ranks sufficient on their tasks. Training runs to at most 4,000 steps (64,000 examples) with early stopping every 100 steps (patience 10) on the mean of three dev scores: exact match, refusal of dev negatives, and exact match on dev corrections. The learning rate is chosen per model and format from {104, 2104, 5104} by dev exact match at pool of 100k over 3 seeds, then frozen (Appendix Table 8). The token cap per format is 1.25 times its longest target, so no correct output can be truncated. Grid. Since no run sees more than 64,000 examples, the larger sizes differ in the diversity of the pool run samples from, not in examples seen; we call the axis pool size. Metrics. sections.title: 6 Results
sections.content: Table 2 gives the full-pool results. On both models WORDS has the highest exact match (87.5% on Qwen; EXR, TAGGED not separable from it) and the lowest silent rate (no other format separable on Qwen; DSL on LFM2), with the fewest tokens on Qwen and nearly the fewest on LFM2. For reference, the published BART-Large EXR system reaches 78.6% on this test set with the full pool (Arkoudas et al., 2022); it is fully fine-tuned encoder-decoder trained without refusals or corrections, so we do not compare further.

sections.title: 6.1 Shorter is not better
sections.content: Regressing exact match on output tokens across the four ladder formats gives positive slope (removing tokens lowers accuracy) in 10 of 10 modelsize cells, never more than 1.1 points per ten tokens, and it separates in only 1. The ladder is not monotone (Figure 2): EXR-SHORT, which only renames EXRs constructors, loses 10.6 points on Qwen, separating at every size, and 3.2 on LFM2; TAGGED, half as long as EXR, matches it on Qwen. Length does not predict accuracy in either direction.

sections.title: 6.2 Surface form, not length
sections.content: The matched pairs separate the two explanations  (Table 3)  . WORDS and DSL share their structure Figure 3: Where the test orders go at the full pool (axis starts at 60%). Labels: silent error rate S. and differ by less than token; they differ only in whether marker is +cheese or extra cheese. WORDS is ahead in every one of the 10 cells, by +7.8 points on Qwen [+6.1, +9.5] and +5.4 on LFM2 at the full pool, and separates in all but one. On LFM2 the pairs token order inverts: WORDS emits 12.0 tokens against DSLs 11.4 and is still the more accurate. format that is longer and more accurate is not winning by being short. EXR and JSON are both bracket-heavy notations, so this pair varies little along the natural-word axis. EXR is ahead in all 10 cells but separates in only 3 (all on Qwen): consistent but small effect, as expected if what matters is words rather than brackets. Against the native format, WORDS is ahead on both models (+1.8 and +3.4 points at the full pool), separating in some sizes on LFM2 and none on Qwen; we read this as matching EXRs accuracy with 4.1 fewer tokens, not as beating it.

sections.title: 6.3 Silent errors and where they come from
sections.content: Exact match and silent rate rank formats differently (Figure 3). EXR and JSON almost always parse, so nearly everything they get wrong they get wrong silently. WORDS and DSL fail to parse more often, and those failures are visible. WORDS has the lowest S: 4.5% against 10.3% for EXR on Qwen, ratio of 2.3 [1.8, 3.1], and 10.0% against 17.9% on LFM2, ratio 1.8 [1.4, 2.3]. The difference separates at every pool size on both models (Table 3, last rows). WORDS also invents fewer entities that the customer never said: 5.5 fewer than EXR on Qwen and 2.4 on LFM2. sections.title: 6.4 The guardrail: refusing and listening
sections.content: Refusal works for every format. Held-out negatives, built from vocabulary never seen in training, are refused 95.999.0% of the time on Qwen and 97.298.3% on LFM2  (Table 4)  . Chatter, gibberish and long text are refused essentially always; the hardest kind is real order with one unknown word, refused 8696% of the time on Qwen (Appendix Figure 4: Silent errors by kind at the full pool, as share of all test orders (bar height = S). Negation: NOT attribute added, lost or misplaced; line count: wrong number of pizzas or drinks. Table 9). Format barely matters here. The price is refusing real orders. 2.15.4% of real test orders are refused on Qwen and 6.310.1% on LFM2. Reading them, they are genuine orders in human phrasing the synthetic grammar never produces: greetings, thanks, and stories (im having bunch of people over tonight so need five pizzas. . . ). Almost every refused order contains word the training grammar never uses (96100% on Qwen, 97100% on LFM2), against 81% of the orders answered. An order with greeting, please or thanks (289 of the test orders) is refused 6.1% of the time by Qwen WORDS against 2.6% for other orders. The strict rule meets politeness the training grammar does not contain.

sections.title: 6.6 Latency
sections.content: Median latency at batch size one is linear in output tokens (Qwen: 29 ms + 26.5 ms per token, R2=1.00; Appendix Figure 6) with throughput flat across formats, so WORDS answers 3.7 faster than EXR on Qwen and 4.4 on LFM2. The processs GPU memory moves only between 1,704 and 1,806 MiB on Qwen: format buys latency and accuracy, not memory.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Which metric, when. If parsers output is acted on without review, is the number that matters: format with higher but higher ships more wrong orders. is the right number to compare with prior work, and Dparse + Drefuse is what retry or human fallback has to absorb. On PIZZA the three point the same way for WORDS, which need not hold elsewhere; reporting all four outcomes makes the trade visible. What transfers. The recipe is to compress the structure of the target and keep its vocabulary natural. It costs nothing at inference, needs no new labels, and is measurable on any parser with the four-way split. Whether the gap persists for larger models and other tasks is open (Limitations). Strict refusal. Refusing anything that is not purely an order keeps the consumer from trusting half ticket, at the cost of 2.110.1% of real orders. Figure 5: Exact match by training pool size, 95% bootstrap bands. Corrections are learned, and best by WORDS. On test orders with held-out cue phrases, exact match is 62.975.3% on Qwen and 49.262.6% on LFM2, and the correction itself is applied in 8088% and 7278% of cases. WORDS is the best format on both models, separating from every other format on LFM2. The reported cheese failure is fixed in 60 of 60 full-pool runs. Training cues score 59 points above held-out cues on Qwen, so part of what is learned is the phrasing of the cue.

sections.title: 6.5 Pool size
sections.content: WORDS is the most accurate format at every pool size on both models (Figure 5). Its lead over EXR is largest at 1k (+4.0 points on Qwen, +7.2 on LFM2) and narrows with pool size; its lead over DSL does not narrow on Qwen (+6.7 at 1k, +7.8 at the full 6 softer rule, or negatives written in human rather than grammar style, could lower that cost; we leave it to future work and report the strict rules price as is.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Output format is free design variable for finetuned parser. On PIZZA, with two model families, five pool sizes and five seeds, writing the target in plain words matches or beats the native formats accuracy with quarter of the tokens and roughly halves the errors nobody can detect, mostly by getting negation right. The gain survives refusal and self-correction guardrail trained into every run, and tokenizer under which the word form is the longer one.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: One dataset. All results are on PIZZA, whose training pool comes from grammar with small vocabulary; the human-written test set is the main guard against learning the grammar alone. Small models. Both models are under billion parameters; the effect may shrink with scale. Authorgenerated guardrail data. Negatives, corrections and probes are generated or written by us, and the human test set contains neither; 32 test orders (2.4%) use make it, make that or hold on in PIZZAs own sense, which our generator teaches as correction cues, bounding any effect on test exact match at 2.4 points. Every run includes the guardrail, so this campaign does not measure what the guardrail costs in accuracy. Tuning. Three learning rates were at the edge of the grid (Appendix Table 8); rank was not tuned; 8 of 300 runs (all LFM2) reached their best checkpoint within 100 steps of the step limit. Generation. 19 of 511,500 generations hit the token cap, all runaway outputs longer than any correct ticket. Deployment. The exported LFM2 GGUF agrees with its trained run on 93% of orders; no number in this paper comes from GGUF.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: PIZZA is released under CC-BY-NC-4.0 and contains no personal data; we redistribute no dataset text. All runs used two NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs. parser that refuses real orders shifts work to staff or customers; we report that rate rather than hide it.

sections.title: A Additional Results
sections.content: Tables 5 to 11 and Figure 6 give the numbers behind Section 6 at every pool size and by kind. All are generated from the run outputs by the scripts in https://github.com/UmarGit/coffee-llm.

sections.title: B Integrity Checks
sections.content: Before reading any result we checked: all 300 runs complete; exact match and parse validity recomputed from the raw outputs with the datasets matcher equal the stored values in every run; negatives and corrections identical across models, formats and sizes for seed; no evaluation utterance in any training subset; batched and batch-one generation agree on all but at most 2 of 200 utterances per run; left padding in every run. The analysis code and the checks are in https://github.com/ UmarGit/coffee-llm.
